title: Anal Cancer
subtitle: StewardMD ONCOTREE navigator (draft)
provenanceNote: DRAFT decision support authored from standard guidelines (NCCN/DeVita/Harrison) - the physician decides. Full pathway: workup and biomarkers -> histology gate (non-squamous routed off-pathway by subtype) -> HIV/immune optimisation -> extent of disease -> localized (local excision -> pathology-adapted; or definitive chemoradiation -> response-adapted restaging -> surveillance vs salvage) / metastatic (biomarker -> line-of-therapy sub-tree: first-line by fitness -> progression -> second-line by immunotherapy eligibility -> later-line) / recurrence (locoregional salvage vs distant). Each treatment leaf routes to APPLICABLE existing StewardMD Standard Protocols only where a same-disease dose protocol exists; radiation, surgery, immunotherapy, DCF and reduced-intensity options are shown as checklist guidance with NO invented dose. Not clinically activated; the existing dose engine computes patient doses.
sourceNote: Structural pathway consistent with Standard Guidelines (NCCN), Anal Carcinoma, and general oncology references (DeVita, Harrison). No proprietary guideline text reproduced. Invents no dose/regimen; the dose engine computes patient doses for referenced protocols.

a.text: Test DPYD before any fluoropyrimidine; a deficient variant sharply raises 5-FU toxicity and warrants dose reduction or avoidance.

b.text: Anal squamous cancer is HPV-driven in most cases; p16 immunostaining is a surrogate for high-risk HPV and carries a favourable prognosis. Assess HIV status, which affects treatment tolerance rather than regimen choice.

c.text: Carboplatin plus paclitaxel is a reasonable first-line doublet for metastatic anal squamous cancer, with a more favourable tolerability profile than cisplatin-fluorouracil in frontline randomized data.

d.text: After definitive chemoradiation, tumour regression may continue for up to 6 months; biopsy only for progression or clearly persistent disease, since early biopsy of a regressing tumour can mislead.

e.text: Checkpoint inhibitors show activity in previously treated anal squamous cancer; MMR-deficient/MSI-high or high PD-L1 status further strengthens the case for immunotherapy.

nodes.name: Initial workup
nodes.title: Initial workup and staging evaluation
nodes.description: Baseline evaluation before treatment: confirm tissue diagnosis, map local extent, and screen for distant disease.
bullets: History and exam including digital rectal exam and anoscopy; document tumour size, distance from anal verge, and sphincter involvement
Inguinal node exam; biopsy or FNA of suspicious groin nodes
Pelvic MRI for primary and nodal extent; CT chest/abdomen/pelvis or PET/CT to screen for distant metastases
HIV test; if positive, obtain CD4 count and involve HIV care. Women: cervical/vulvar screening given shared HPV aetiology
Baseline CBC and renal/hepatic function; DPYD testing before any fluoropyrimidine (footnote a)

nodes.name: Biomarkers
nodes.title: Biomarker and host-factor assessment
nodes.description: Anal squamous cancer has few regimen-directing molecular gates; these markers inform prognosis, later-line options, and safety.
bullets: p16/HPV: prognostic; most anal squamous cancers are HPV-associated and p16-positive tumours respond better
HIV status and CD4: affects tolerance and supportive care, not first-regimen choice
MMR/MSI and PD-L1 (CPS): relevant to later-line immunotherapy decisions
DPYD: safety gate before fluorouracil (footnote a)

tables.title: Biomarker panel and its role
rows: Prognostic; p16-positive tends to respond better
Supports checkpoint-inhibitor consideration in advanced disease
Deficiency requires 5-FU dose reduction or avoidance

nodes.name: Histology
nodes.title: Histology gate
nodes.description: This navigator covers anal squamous cell carcinoma. Non-squamous histologies follow a different pathway by subtype.

nodes.name: Non-squamous subtype
nodes.title: Non-squamous: route by subtype
nodes.description: Non-squamous histologies are not managed by the anal squamous chemoradiation algorithm; select the subtype to route to the correct disease pathway.

nodes.name: Adenocarcinoma - off pathway
nodes.title: Anal adenocarcinoma: manage as rectal adenocarcinoma
nodes.description: Glandular histology behaves like a low rectal cancer.
bullets: Treat like a rectal adenocarcinoma: neoadjuvant chemoradiation or total neoadjuvant therapy, then radical surgery
Systemic chemotherapy (fluoropyrimidine/oxaliplatin based) by stage and MMR status
Re-enter the colorectal/rectal disease navigator for staging and dosing

nodes.name: Anorectal melanoma - off pathway
nodes.title: Anorectal melanoma: melanoma pathway
nodes.description: A biologically distinct, often aggressive mucosal melanoma.
bullets: Wide local excision with sphincter preservation where feasible; radical surgery rarely improves survival
Systemic checkpoint immunotherapy and targeted therapy per the melanoma pathway
Re-enter the melanoma navigator for staging and dosing

nodes.name: Neuroendocrine / GIST - off pathway
nodes.title: Neuroendocrine or GIST: histology-specific pathway
nodes.description: Manage on the tumour-type-specific pathway.
bullets: Grade/differentiation-directed therapy for neuroendocrine tumours; imatinib-based therapy for GIST
Re-enter the neuroendocrine or GIST navigator for staging and dosing

nodes.name: HIV / immune status
nodes.title: HIV and immune status
nodes.description: HIV-positive patients tolerate curative chemoradiation but need closer toxicity management; regimen intent is unchanged.
bullets: Continue antiretroviral therapy through treatment; coordinate with HIV care
Expect more acute skin/mucosal toxicity; do not reflexively de-intensify curative therapy
Optimise CD4 and manage opportunistic-infection risk

nodes.name: HIV optimisation
nodes.title: HIV-positive: optimise before curative therapy
nodes.description: Optimise immune and antiretroviral status so full-intent chemoradiation can proceed on schedule.
bullets: Confirm antiretroviral adherence and suppressed viral load; involve HIV specialist co-management
Prophylaxis for opportunistic infection if CD4 is low; baseline dermatology/perineal skin plan
Plan intensive supportive care (skin, mucosa, marrow) rather than a lower radiation or chemotherapy dose
Proceed to extent-of-disease assessment once optimised

nodes.name: Extent of disease
nodes.title: Extent of disease
nodes.description: Choose the current clinical scenario; this sets the treatment intent.

nodes.name: Localized stage
nodes.title: Localized: stage and local extent
nodes.description: Stratify localized disease. Nearly all invasive anal squamous cancer is treated with organ-preserving chemoradiation; only small, well-differentiated anal-margin tumours are candidates for local excision alone.
bullets: Local excision candidate: small superficial well-differentiated anal-margin lesion, node-negative, adequate margins achievable without sphincter loss
Stage I-II: invasive primary, clinically node-negative (N0)
Stage III: node-positive (perirectal/internal iliac/inguinal) or locally advanced primary (T4)

options.label: Early anal-margin lesion - local excision candidate

nodes.name: Local excision
nodes.title: Early anal-margin lesion: local excision
nodes.description: Wide local excision for selected small, well-differentiated, node-negative anal-margin tumours; pathology then dictates the next step.
bullets: Wide local excision aiming for clear margins with sphincter preservation
No systemic therapy for a completely excised early lesion
Review final pathology (margin status, depth, differentiation) before deciding on surveillance vs chemoradiation (next step)

nodes.name: Excision pathology
nodes.title: Post-excision pathology: adequacy
nodes.description: Final pathology after local excision determines whether surveillance is sufficient or definitive chemoradiation is needed.
bullets: Clear margins (>=1 mm), superficial, well-differentiated, node-negative: surveillance alone is appropriate
Positive/close margins, deeper invasion, or upstaging: proceed to definitive chemoradiation
Re-excision is an option only if it will not compromise sphincter function

options.label: Clear margins - fully excised early lesion

nodes.name: Post-excision surveillance
nodes.title: Fully excised early lesion: surveillance
nodes.description: Adequately excised early anal-margin lesion; no further treatment.
bullets: Clinical exam, DRE, and anoscopy every 3-6 months for 2-3 years, then less often to 5 years
Re-examine the excision site for local recurrence; low threshold to re-biopsy a new nodule
Manage HPV-related field risk (anal/cervical/vulvar screening)
Re-enter the recurrence pathway on any confirmed relapse

nodes.name: Nodal management
nodes.title: Node-positive: nodal radiation planning
nodes.description: Node-positive disease is treated with definitive chemoradiation that covers involved and at-risk nodal basins, with a boost to gross nodes.
bullets: Cover pelvic and inguinal nodal regions in the radiation field
Boost gross nodal disease to a higher dose
Elective groin irradiation rather than upfront dissection for most node-positive cases
Reserve node dissection for residual/recurrent groin disease after chemoradiation

options.label: Nodal plan reviewed - continue to chemoradiation

nodes.name: Chemo fitness
nodes.title: Definitive chemoradiation: mitomycin fitness
nodes.description: Mitomycin plus fluorouracil with concurrent radiation is the standard backbone. Choose the concurrent chemotherapy by marrow, renal, and general fitness.
bullets: Standard backbone: fluorouracil + mitomycin with concurrent radiation (organ-preserving)
Assess marrow reserve (mitomycin myelosuppression) and renal function
Confirm DPYD before fluorouracil (footnote a)

nodes.name: 5FU-MMC chemoRT
nodes.title: Definitive chemoradiation: fluorouracil + mitomycin
nodes.description: Standard organ-preserving definitive treatment for localized anal squamous carcinoma; response is then assessed on a defined schedule.
bullets: Fluorouracil + mitomycin delivered concurrently with a single definitive radiation course
Radiation field covers primary and at-risk/involved nodes; boost gross disease
Manage radiation dermatitis/proctitis and mitomycin myelosuppression; avoid treatment breaks where possible
Proceed to response-adapted restaging at about 8-12 weeks and again toward 6 months (next step, footnote d)

nodes.name: chemoRT alternative
nodes.title: Definitive chemoradiation without mitomycin
nodes.description: For patients unsuitable for mitomycin (marrow suppression, significant comorbidity); same radiation intent and response schedule.
bullets: Substitute a cisplatin-based fluoropyrimidine backbone concurrent with radiation where mitomycin is contraindicated
For frail patients, consider radiation with a reduced-intensity fluoropyrimidine, or radiation alone if chemotherapy is unsafe
No mitomycin-substitution dose protocol here - the physician selects and doses the concurrent agent
Proceed to the same response-adapted restaging as the standard backbone (next step)

nodes.name: Response / restaging
nodes.title: Post-treatment response and restaging
nodes.description: After definitive chemoradiation (or at a surveillance visit), assess with clinical exam, DRE, anoscopy, and imaging. Regression can continue for months; act on the confirmed pattern.
bullets: DRE, anoscopy, and inguinal node exam every 3-6 months for the first 2-3 years
Pelvic MRI and chest/abdomen/pelvis imaging periodically per risk
Biopsy only for progression or clearly persistent disease (footnote d)

nodes.name: Complete response
nodes.title: Complete response: continued surveillance
nodes.description: Sustained complete response after definitive therapy.
bullets: Continue exam, DRE, and anoscopy every 3-6 months for 2-3 years, then less often to 5 years
Periodic imaging for patients who were node-positive or locally advanced
Manage late radiation effects (proctitis, sexual/urinary dysfunction, marrow)
Re-enter the recurrence pathway on any confirmed relapse

nodes.name: Persistent-disease evaluation
nodes.title: Persistent disease: regressing vs confirmed
nodes.description: Distinguish ongoing regression from true persistent disease before committing to salvage surgery.
bullets: Serial exam and MRI over weeks; regression may continue up to 6 months post-chemoradiation
Biopsy to confirm before salvage surgery (footnote d)

nodes.name: Close observation
nodes.title: Regressing tumour: close observation
nodes.description: Incompletely regressed but still improving after chemoradiation.
bullets: Re-examine and re-image at short intervals up to 6 months post-treatment
Avoid premature biopsy or salvage surgery while the tumour is still regressing
Proceed to salvage evaluation only if disease fails to clear or progresses (footnote d)

nodes.name: Salvage assessment
nodes.title: Locoregional salvage: resectability
nodes.description: Assess whether locoregional recurrent or persistent disease is resectable for cure by abdominoperineal resection.
bullets: Multidisciplinary review; confirm no distant disease before radical surgery
Assess sphincter involvement, pelvic sidewall fixation, and fitness for major surgery

nodes.name: Salvage APR
nodes.title: Salvage abdominoperineal resection
nodes.description: Potentially curative surgery for resectable locoregional recurrence or persistent disease after chemoradiation.
bullets: Abdominoperineal resection with permanent colostomy; consider plastic reconstruction of the perineum
Manage groin recurrence with therapeutic inguinal node dissection as indicated
Adjuvant systemic therapy is not standard; individualise by pathology
Enter surveillance after recovery; re-enter the recurrence pathway on relapse

nodes.name: Unresectable salvage
nodes.title: Unresectable locoregional recurrence: non-surgical salvage
nodes.description: Locoregional recurrence not amenable to, or patient unfit for, salvage surgery.
bullets: Consider selective re-irradiation at experienced centres where prior dose allows
Systemic therapy per the metastatic pathway for uncontrolled locoregional disease
Palliative measures for symptom control including a diverting stoma if needed
Discuss clinical-trial options

nodes.name: Metastatic workup
nodes.title: Metastatic / advanced disease workup
nodes.description: Confirm and characterise metastatic disease before selecting systemic therapy.
bullets: Biopsy a metastatic site if diagnosis or histology is uncertain
Full restaging imaging (CT chest/abdomen/pelvis or PET/CT)
Assess performance status and organ function for regimen fitness
Confirm DPYD before any fluoropyrimidine (footnote a)

nodes.name: Advanced biomarkers
nodes.title: Advanced disease: immunotherapy biomarkers
nodes.description: Confirm the biomarkers that will steer later-line therapy before committing to a first-line plan.
bullets: MMR/MSI: MSI-high predicts checkpoint-inhibitor benefit and may justify earlier immunotherapy
PD-L1 (CPS): supports checkpoint-inhibitor selection in later lines
p16/HPV status for prognosis; germline/HIV context for tolerance
Results rarely change first-line cytotoxic choice but front-load the later-line decision (footnote e)

nodes.name: First-line fitness
nodes.title: Metastatic first-line: fitness
nodes.description: Select first-line systemic therapy by fitness for a platinum doublet.

nodes.name: First-line doublet
nodes.title: Fit first-line: choose the doublet
nodes.description: Both are reasonable frontline options; carboplatin-paclitaxel is generally preferred for tolerability, with DCF reserved for very fit patients seeking maximal response.

nodes.name: Carbo-paclitaxel
nodes.title: Metastatic first-line: carboplatin + paclitaxel
nodes.description: Preferred first-line doublet for fit patients with metastatic anal squamous carcinoma.
bullets: Carboplatin + paclitaxel is the preferred frontline doublet (better tolerated than cisplatin-fluorouracil)
Reassess with imaging every 2-3 cycles; continue to progression or unacceptable toxicity
Then move to the progression assessment (next step) to time later-line therapy

nodes.name: DCF
nodes.title: Metastatic first-line: docetaxel + cisplatin + fluorouracil
nodes.description: A more intensive frontline triplet for very fit patients seeking maximal response.
bullets: Modified DCF (docetaxel, cisplatin, fluorouracil) offers high response rates at the cost of more toxicity
Reserve for excellent performance status; use growth-factor support and confirm DPYD (footnote a)
No anal-specific DCF dose protocol here - the physician selects and doses the triplet
Then move to the progression assessment (next step)

nodes.name: Reduced-intensity systemic
nodes.title: Metastatic, frail: reduced-intensity systemic therapy
nodes.description: First-line for patients unfit for a full platinum doublet.
bullets: Single-agent or dose-attenuated therapy (a fluoropyrimidine, or a reduced carboplatin-paclitaxel schedule)
Checkpoint-inhibitor monotherapy may suit selected patients who cannot tolerate cytotoxics
Prioritise symptom control and quality of life; no reduced-dose protocol referenced here
Then move to the progression assessment (next step)

nodes.name: First-line outcome
nodes.title: After first-line: response vs progression
nodes.description: First-line outcome directs whether to continue/maintain or move to a later line.

nodes.name: Continue / maintenance
nodes.title: Responding disease: continue therapy
nodes.description: Ongoing response or stable disease on first-line systemic therapy.
bullets: Continue the effective regimen to progression or cumulative toxicity (e.g. platinum/taxane neuropathy)
Consider a treatment holiday or a maintenance fluoropyrimidine for durable responders
Re-image every 2-3 cycles; re-enter the later-line pathway at progression
Integrate palliative care for symptom burden

nodes.name: Second-line eligibility
nodes.title: Second-line: immunotherapy eligibility
nodes.description: After platinum progression, checkpoint inhibition is a recognised option; some patients are better served by other cytotoxics or supportive care.
bullets: Checkpoint inhibitors show activity in previously treated anal squamous cancer (footnote e)
MSI-high / high PD-L1 strengthen the case for immunotherapy
Weigh performance status and autoimmune history

nodes.name: Immunotherapy
nodes.title: Second-line: checkpoint immunotherapy
nodes.description: Previously treated metastatic anal squamous carcinoma, immunotherapy-eligible.
bullets: Anti-PD-1 monotherapy (e.g. pembrolizumab or nivolumab) after platinum progression
Monitor for immune-related adverse events; no anal-specific immunotherapy dose protocol here
Continue to progression or unacceptable toxicity
On progression, move to the later-line assessment (next step)

nodes.name: Second-line cytotoxic
nodes.title: Second-line: alternative cytotoxic therapy
nodes.description: Second-line when immunotherapy is unsuitable.
bullets: A taxane or fluoropyrimidine-based regimen not previously used, or re-challenge if durable prior benefit
No later-line dose protocol referenced here - the physician selects and doses the agent
Integrate palliative care alongside systemic therapy
On progression, move to the later-line assessment (next step)

nodes.name: Later-line decision
nodes.title: Third-line and beyond: trial vs supportive care
nodes.description: After two prior lines, weigh a further systemic line or a clinical trial against a supportive-care-only approach.

options.label: Fit for a further line / clinical trial

nodes.name: Third-line / trial
nodes.title: Third-line and beyond: further systemic therapy or trial
nodes.description: A further systemic line or clinical trial for patients retaining good performance status.
bullets: Prioritise clinical-trial enrolment where available (novel HPV-directed or checkpoint combinations)
Otherwise a single agent not previously used, chosen for tolerability
No later-line dose protocol referenced here - the physician selects and doses the agent
Reassess performance status frequently; transition to supportive care when the burden outweighs benefit

nodes.name: Supportive care
nodes.title: Best supportive / palliative care
nodes.description: Poor performance status where anticancer therapy offers little benefit.
bullets: Symptom-directed care: pain, local hygiene, bleeding, stoma needs
Early specialist palliative-care involvement
Palliative radiation for symptomatic local or metastatic sites
Reassess for systemic therapy if performance status improves

nodes.name: Recurrence pattern
nodes.title: Recurrence after definitive therapy
nodes.description: Restage to distinguish locoregional-only recurrence (potentially salvageable by surgery) from distant disease.
bullets: Biopsy to confirm recurrence; PET/CT and pelvic MRI to define extent
Locoregional-only recurrence may be curable with salvage surgery
Distant disease follows the metastatic pathway
